paragraphs: Curriculum learning changes which examples a model sees during training, often following an easy-to-hard schedule. The difficulty is deciding what makes an example easy or useful at a particular stage. This paper reframes that choice as an adaptive decision problem: the training process learns which selection strategy to use as it proceeds.

The proposed method, OnlineSubmod, treats each submodular function for choosing a training subset as an arm in a multi-armed bandit. Its online greedy policy receives a utility-based reward, allowing feedback to guide subsequent choices. The authors particularly emphasize rewards derived from validation performance as a principled way to shape the curriculum.

The paper proves no-regret performance under several sampling regimes, providing theoretical support for the adaptive selection policy. Experiments on vision and language datasets report better accuracy-efficiency tradeoffs than traditional curricula and approaches based on bilevel optimization. The contribution connects subset selection with measurable training benefits, reducing dependence on a predetermined notion of sample difficulty.
neurips-2025-bandit-guided-submodular-cu.tldr: OnlineSubmod learns which training-subset selection strategy to use through bandit feedback, improving reported accuracy-efficiency tradeoffs.

paragraphs: Multimodal dataset distillation compresses a large image-text dataset into a small substitute that remains useful for learning relationships between images and language. This paper identifies a failure called modality collapse: representations within each modality become overly concentrated, while the gap between image and text distributions grows. The authors attribute this to tension between aggressive compression and contrastive supervision across modalities.

RepBlend addresses that tension by blending representations, weakening overly dominant cross-modal supervision and increasing diversity within each modality. A second component tackles unequal supervision of images and text. Symmetric projection trajectory matching uses separate projection heads to coordinate their optimization dynamics, supporting more balanced learning and better alignment.

On Flickr-30K and MS-COCO, RepBlend consistently improves over the prior state-of-the-art methods evaluated. Reported gains include +9.4 IR@10 and +6.3 TR@10 with 100 image-text pairs, alongside distillation speedups reaching 6.7 times. These findings support preserving representation diversity and balancing supervision as complementary ways to make very small multimodal training sets more effective.
neurips-2025-beyond-modality-collapse-re.tldr: RepBlend improves multimodal dataset distillation by preserving representation diversity and balancing supervision between images and text.

paragraphs: A user instruction can contain several requirements that broad reward criteria such as helpfulness do not describe individually. This paper proposes Reinforcement Learning from Checklist Feedback, or RLCF, to make training rewards reflect the particular requirements of each instruction. The central idea is to judge a response against a tailored checklist.

RLCF extracts checklist items from instructions, then evaluates how well responses satisfy them. It uses both AI judges and specialized verification programs, combining their item-level scores into a reinforcement-learning reward. This gives the training process a way to respond to multiple needs expressed within the same query.

Starting from Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, RLCF was the only compared alignment method to improve all five evaluated benchmarks. Reported gains include four points in FollowBench hard satisfaction rate, six points on InFoBench, and three points in Arena-Hard win rate. Off-policy use also improved Llama 3.1 8B Instruct and OLMo 2 7B Instruct. The results support instruction-specific rubrics as a useful alignment tool, with the WildChecklists dataset, models, and code released publicly.
neurips-2025-checklists-are-better-than-.tldr: RLCF turns instruction-specific checklists into reinforcement-learning rewards and improves all five evaluated benchmarks on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct.

paragraphs: Federated LoRA lets users jointly fine-tune a language model by exchanging small adaptor updates while keeping raw data local. Those updates can still leak private information. Adding differential privacy creates a particular difficulty: applying noise to both low-rank adaptor matrices amplifies noise in the model, while holding one matrix fixed restricts what fine-tuning can learn.

FedASK addresses this tradeoff with a two-stage sketching procedure inspired by randomized singular value decomposition. It first aggregates carefully constructed, privacy-preserving sketches of local updates. The server then reconstructs the global matrices, allowing both adaptor matrices to be updated within the proposed privacy framework.

The authors prove differential privacy and an exact aggregation property for FedASK. Experiments report consistent improvements over the evaluated baselines across multiple privacy settings and data distributions. The contribution is a way to reconcile privacy with the flexibility of updating both matrices, rather than accepting the learning restriction introduced by fixing one of them.
neurips-2025-differentially-private-fede.tldr: FedASK uses two-stage sketching to update both federated LoRA matrices with proven differential privacy and improved reported performance.

paragraphs: When a machine-learning model influences resource allocation, affected people or organizations may change their recorded features to obtain better outcomes. Such changes can reflect real adaptation or deceptive reporting, and observing changed features alone does not separate the two. This paper develops a causal method for estimating how much misreporting occurs on average.

The method relies on a specific asymmetry: a genuine change can affect downstream variables, whereas merely misreporting a feature does not causally change those descendants. The authors compare causal effects derived from manipulated data with those derived from unmanipulated data. That comparison provides a basis for distinguishing reported changes from changes that propagate through the underlying causal system.

The paper proves that the misreporting rate is identifiable in its formulation and characterizes the estimator's variance. Empirical checks use semi-synthetic data and a real Medicare dataset containing misreported data. These results support using downstream causal relationships to quantify misreporting in strategic settings, with the target being an average rate rather than a claim to classify every individual report.
neurips-2025-disentangling-misreporting-.tldr: The paper estimates average misreporting by comparing how reported features relate causally to downstream variables in manipulated and unmanipulated data.

paragraphs: Many stochastic processes have memory: changes at different times are correlated, sometimes over long intervals. Standard diffusion bridges driven by Brownian motion do not capture the temporal dependencies, roughness, and anomalous diffusion described here. Fractional Diffusion Bridge Models introduce fractional Brownian motion to represent this richer behavior.

The framework uses a recent Markovian approximation to make inference tractable while retaining the non-Markovian character of fractional Brownian motion. The authors prove that the resulting bridge preserves the coupling between its endpoints and use it to predict future states from paired training examples. They also extend the formulation to the Schrödinger bridge problem, deriving a training loss for translation between unpaired datasets.

Evaluation covers future protein conformation prediction with aligned data and unpaired image translation. Relative to Brownian baselines, the method achieves lower deviation of protein C-alpha atomic positions and lower Fréchet Inception Distance for images. These findings show benefits from the proposed framework in both paired prediction and unpaired translation, supporting its use beyond a single application.
neurips-2025-fractional-diffusion-bridge.tldr: Fractional Diffusion Bridge Models incorporate temporal memory into tractable generative bridges and outperform Brownian baselines on two evaluated tasks.

paragraphs: An image search query may depend on a particular visual attribute that a general image representation does not emphasize. To study this problem, the authors create COCO-Facet, a benchmark containing 9,112 attribute-focused queries. They find weak and uneven performance from CLIP-like retrievers, with similar difficulties persisting in stronger multimodal language-model retrievers.

The paper suggests that general embeddings may prioritize overall meaning and main subjects while overlooking other details. It proposes promptable image embeddings that highlight the attributes needed for a query. The embedding-generation pipeline shows generalization across query types, image collections, and underlying retriever architectures.

Two acceleration strategies address different deployment conditions. Precomputing promptable embeddings applies when prompts are known beforehand, while linear approximations support prompts supplied during inference. The authors report Recall@5 improvements of 15% and 8%, respectively. The findings support adapting image representations to the requested attributes; the proposed explanation for why general embeddings struggle remains a hypothesis rather than a settled causal conclusion.
neurips-2025-highlighting-what-matters-p.tldr: Promptable image embeddings improve attribute-focused retrieval by emphasizing query-relevant details, with acceleration options for predefined and inference-time prompts.

paragraphs: Model merging combines pretrained models to broaden their capabilities. Most methods concentrate on combining parameter values within matching architectures. This paper also explores how layers can be assembled into inference paths, a harder search problem because the number of possible arrangements is large and layer compatibility must be considered.

HM3 organizes the problem into two levels with multiple objectives. At the parameter level, it incorporates existing merging methods to identify useful parameter combinations. At the architecture level, an actor-critic strategy searches paths through layers, using efficient policy discretization and paths with the Markov property. The two levels connect parameter choices with architectural reconstruction.

Reusable policy and value networks are trained to find Pareto-optimal models: solutions representing different tradeoffs among objectives. This supports customized choices for different tasks rather than requiring one universal compromise. Experiments on language and vision tasks report better performance than methods searching only parameters or only architectures. The results support coordinating the two search spaces, while making clear that HM3 itself trains networks to guide that search.
neurips-2025-hm3-hierarchical-multi-obje.tldr: HM3 jointly searches parameter combinations and layer-level inference paths to produce merged models with different task tradeoffs.

paragraphs: Domain generalization asks whether training across several data distributions can produce a model that works on distributions it has not seen. This paper focuses on the number of domains needed, rather than only the amount of data. Its target is reasonable performance on every domain in a specified family, including those absent from training.

The authors formalize this question in the probably approximately correct, or PAC, framework, with training domains sampled randomly. They introduce the domain shattering dimension, a combinatorial measure that characterizes domain sample complexity. This gives the question a mathematical answer tied to a measure of complexity, rather than a fixed number of domains that would apply to every learning problem.

The paper also establishes a tight quantitative relationship with the classical VC dimension. Through that connection, it shows that every hypothesis class learnable in the standard PAC setting is learnable in this domain-generalization setting. The conclusion concerns the stated family of distributions and sampling formulation, giving a theoretical learnability result within that framework.
neurips-2025-how-many-domains-suffice-fo.tldr: The domain shattering dimension tightly characterizes how many randomly sampled domains suffice for learning across a specified domain family.

paragraphs: Sequential recommenders learn from interaction histories, but users and items with few interactions receive much less training evidence. Transferring knowledge from frequently observed data can help, yet a large representational gap can make that transfer harmful. The paper also argues that informal head-versus-tail divisions miss important properties of the data distribution.

HPSERec uses a data imbalance metric to partition items into a hierarchy of subsets. Each subset receives an expert network that learns user-specific local features. Knowledge distillation then improves representations of long-tail interests progressively, creating intermediate stages for transferring information across the hierarchy.

A feedback module based on Sinkhorn optimal transport aligns user representations across expert levels through a globally optimal, soft matching. This alignment complements the staged distillation by connecting representations learned in different subsets. Experiments on three real-world datasets report consistent improvements over all evaluated baselines. The findings support combining distribution-aware partitioning, gradual enhancement, and representation alignment to address the difficulties of direct head-to-tail transfer.
neurips-2025-hpserec-a-hierarchical-part.tldr: HPSERec improves long-tail sequential recommendation through hierarchical experts, progressive knowledge transfer, and optimal-transport alignment.

paragraphs: Training embodied agents often depends on large amounts of experience or accurate simulators, resources that are unavailable in many real-world situations. Learned world models offer another route: passively collected offline data can support simulated environments in which an agent practices. The central challenge is making the generated experience useful for learning.

Imagined Autocurricula, or IMAC, applies Unsupervised Environment Design to worlds generated by a learned model. This produces an automatic curriculum over those environments. The approach therefore addresses which imagined worlds should shape training, connecting environment generation with the goal of preparing agents for new task variations.

Across challenging procedurally generated environments, agents trained entirely inside a world model show strong transfer to held-out environments. The world model itself was learned from a narrower dataset, making this a demonstration of transfer beyond the variation available in that initial data. The authors present larger foundation world models as a possible future direction; the reported result establishes the approach in the evaluated environment settings.
neurips-2025-imagined-autocurricula-9026.tldr: IMAC automatically organizes imagined training environments into curricula, enabling strong reported transfer from a world model learned on narrower data.

paragraphs: Model-based reinforcement learning uses a learned model of environment dynamics to reason about possible futures. Errors in that model can accumulate during imagined rollouts and affect the resulting policy. This paper studies whether the shape of the model's training loss helps explain and improve downstream control performance.

The method adds Sharpness-Aware Minimization, or SAM, to world-model training while leaving the planner, policy components, and architecture unchanged. SAM encourages flatter minima, where the loss is less sensitive to nearby parameter changes. The authors derive PAC-Bayesian bounds connecting first-order sharpness with errors in value estimation and the performance gap between model-optimal and true-optimal policies; reduced sharpness tightens these bounds.

Experiments on HumanoidBench, Atari-100k, and high-dimensional DeepMind Control tasks show reduced measured sharpness, lower value-prediction error, and improved returns. Gains are especially large in settings with high-dimensional state-action spaces. Positive transfer across algorithms and input modalities, including a transformer world model, supports flatness-aware training as a broadly useful modification within the tested systems.
neurips-2025-improving-model-based-reinf.tldr: Applying SAM to world-model training tightens sharpness-based theoretical bounds and improves control returns across the evaluated reinforcement-learning systems.

paragraphs: Novel view synthesis generates views of a scene from new camera positions, supporting applications such as virtual reality, games, and robotic simulation. Rapid progress in Neural Radiance Fields and 3D Gaussian Splatting has made comparisons difficult. Methods use different evaluation procedures, can be hard to install, and may not generalize well to new scenes.

The authors experimentally show that even small differences in evaluation protocols can artificially improve reported performance. NerfBaselines addresses this problem with consistent benchmarking tools and a framework that simplifies installing and running different methods. The aim is to make numerical comparisons reflect differences between methods more reliably.

To validate the implementation, the authors reproduce results reported in the original papers. They also release a web platform comparing commonly used methods on standard benchmarks. This work contributes evaluation infrastructure rather than a new synthesis model: it connects reproducible implementations with shared measurement procedures, helping researchers assess whether apparent gains represent progress under comparable testing conditions.
neurips-2025-nerfbaselines-consistent-an.tldr: NerfBaselines standardizes novel-view synthesis evaluation after showing that small protocol differences can artificially inflate performance.

paragraphs: A stochastic bandit algorithm learns which choices yield better rewards while making those choices repeatedly. Differential privacy adds a requirement to protect the data informing its decisions. This paper revisits how much regret, or lost reward relative to optimal choices, is unavoidable under epsilon-global differential privacy, closing a gap left by bounds that previously agreed only in order.

The authors strengthen the lower bound using a new information-theoretic quantity that varies with the privacy budget. It interpolates between Kullback–Leibler divergence and total variation distance. They also construct private versions of KL-UCB and IMED using phases specific to each arm and Laplace noise.

For Bernoulli bandits, the proposed algorithms asymptotically match the new lower bound within a factor arbitrarily close to one. The analysis introduces a private counterpart of the Chernoff bound for Bernoulli sums under the Laplace mechanism. Numerical experiments report lower regret than existing epsilon-global private bandit algorithms. The strongest matching result is specifically asymptotic and established for Bernoulli rewards.
neurips-2025-optimal-regret-of-bandits-u.tldr: Private versions of KL-UCB and IMED nearly attain a sharper asymptotic regret lower bound for Bernoulli bandits.

paragraphs: Vision sequence models usually turn an image into patches and read them row by row. Although full self-attention is permutation-equivariant, approximations used in modern long-sequence transformers can make patch order matter. This paper shows that changing the ordering, including using columns or Hilbert curves, can substantially affect accuracy in these settings.

REOrder learns an ordering suited to the task through two stages. First, it measures how compressible different patch sequences are to construct an information-theoretic prior. It then optimizes a Plackett-Luce policy over permutations using REINFORCE, providing a way to search the large space of possible patch arrangements efficiently.

Compared with row-major ordering, the method improves top-1 accuracy by up to 3.01% on ImageNet-1K and by 13.35% on Functional Map of the World. The findings make input serialization a meaningful design choice for the order-sensitive architectures studied. They support learning patch order alongside other modeling choices, with the reported gains arising in settings where architectural approximations make ordering consequential.
neurips-2025-reordering-patches-improves.tldr: REOrder learns image-patch sequences that improve accuracy in vision models whose architectural approximations make them sensitive to patch order.

paragraphs: Spectral decomposition studies an operator through its eigenfunctions, a task relevant to representation learning, dynamical systems, and partial differential equations. Neural networks offer a scalable way to approximate those functions. This paper revisits the orbital minimization method, a classical optimization approach from computational chemistry, as a foundation for that learning process.

The authors provide a simple proof, using linear algebra, that the OMM objective is consistent. They also connect the method with ideas that emerged independently in other fields. These results explain why the older objective has broader relevance and provide a theoretical basis for adapting it to modern learning pipelines.

The framework is then used to train neural networks to decompose positive semidefinite operators. Across a range of benchmark tasks, the authors report practical advantages. The contribution combines a clearer justification of an established numerical method with a neural implementation, showing how classical optimization can support scalable tools for scientific computation and machine learning in the operator setting studied.
neurips-2025-revisiting-orbital-minimiza.tldr: The paper gives a simple consistency proof for orbital minimization and adapts it to neural decomposition of positive semidefinite operators.

paragraphs: Machine unlearning aims to remove the influence of unwanted training data without repeating the entire training process. Certified unlearning adds a formal guarantee, based on differential privacy, about how thoroughly the model weights erase that information. This paper extends the approach to general nonconvex loss functions, beyond the more restrictive settings emphasized in earlier work.

The algorithm rewinds training to an earlier step and then runs gradient descent using only the retained data. It is a first-order, black-box procedure that can apply to models pretrained with vanilla gradient descent. The authors prove epsilon-delta certified unlearning and performance guarantees describing the tradeoff among privacy, utility, and computational complexity.

The paper separately proves generalization guarantees when the nonconvex objective satisfies the Polyak–Lojasiewicz inequality. That additional condition qualifies the generalization result, rather than the entire stated nonconvex scope. Experiments use a new framework intended to better reflect practical user-data removal and report superior performance over existing methods. The contribution combines a rewind-based procedure with explicit guarantees about its costs and benefits.
neurips-2025-rewind-to-delete-certified-.tldr: Rewind-to-Delete provides certified unlearning for general nonconvex losses by restarting from an earlier training step on retained data.

paragraphs: Brain electrodes record electrical activity that must be separated into signals associated with individual neurons. This process, called spike sorting, helps researchers study how neurons communicate and process information. Assessing sorting methods is difficult because real recordings rarely provide the ground-truth labels needed to establish which neuron produced each signal.

The authors explore a data-driven alternative to heuristically designed sorting methods. They first generate a large electrophysiology dataset using biologically realistic computational models. SimSort then uses that simulated dataset for deep-learning-based pretraining, placing simulation at the center of the training approach.

Despite being trained solely on simulated data, SimSort demonstrates zero-shot generalization to real-world spike-sorting tasks. It consistently improves over existing methods across multiple evaluated benchmarks. These findings show that simulation-trained representations can transfer to experimental recordings in the tested settings. They support simulation-driven pretraining as a promising route toward more robust and scalable spike sorting, especially where obtaining real training labels is difficult.
neurips-2025-simsort-a-data-driven-frame.tldr: SimSort learns spike sorting entirely from biologically realistic simulations and shows zero-shot improvements on real-world benchmarks.

paragraphs: Long-context supervised fine-tuning commonly mixes long and short sequences to adapt language models smoothly. That mixture creates a systems problem: existing training systems struggle to process both lengths efficiently within the same workload. As a result, the overall training process can perform worse than its individual components might suggest.

Skrull addresses this through dynamic data scheduling. It balances the computational requirements of long and short sequences as training proceeds. The authors formulate scheduling as a joint optimization problem and analyze its tradeoffs, then use that analysis to design a lightweight online scheduling algorithm with near-zero scheduling cost.

Implemented on top of DeepSpeed, Skrull achieves reported speedups averaging 3.76 times and reaching 7.54 times over DeepSpeed in real-world long-context fine-tuning scenarios. These are improvements in training-system efficiency, addressing the handling of heterogeneous sequence lengths. The contribution shows that coordinating when different examples are processed can substantially improve end-to-end performance without treating the mixed-length dataset merely as a fixed workload.
neurips-2025-skrull-towards-efficient-lo.tldr: Skrull dynamically schedules mixed-length training data, delivering an average 3.76-times speedup over DeepSpeed in evaluated long-context fine-tuning scenarios.

paragraphs: In-context learning lets a transformer adapt to a task using demonstrations in its prompt, without updating its parameters. This paper asks how efficiently those demonstrations are used compared with principled learning algorithms. The relevant issue is sample complexity: how much evidence a learner needs to meet a given performance requirement.

The authors build a meta-learning setup where each prompt specifies a regression task drawn from a hierarchical distribution. Solving a task requires inference about both the underlying model class and its particular parameters. They compare transformer in-context learning with alternatives including the Bayes-optimal estimator while varying the required performance.

The results reveal two regimes. In-context learning initially matches the Bayes-optimal estimator's efficiency, but its efficiency deteriorates with long context. An information-theoretic analysis identifies this diminishing efficiency as inherent to in-context learning in the studied formulation. The finding concerns how effectively additional examples are used; it motivates adaptive methods that could sustain efficiency as more evidence becomes available.
neurips-2025-technical-debt-in-in-contex.tldr: In a hierarchical regression setting, in-context learning initially matches Bayesian sample efficiency but becomes less efficient as context grows.

paragraphs: How test error changes with model complexity depends partly on how complexity is measured. Counting parameters often fails to explain the behavior of large, overparameterized networks. This paper instead studies capacity measures based on model norms, using random-feature estimators as a simplified theoretical setting for understanding more complex networks.

The authors precisely characterize how the estimator's norm concentrates and how it governs test error. Their main mathematical tool is deterministic equivalence, and they develop new deterministic quantities as part of the analysis. This connects a norm-based description of the fitted model with predictions about its generalization behavior.

In this setting, the predicted learning curve has a transition between underparameterization and overparameterization but does not show double descent. Using the norm-based capacity measure recovers a more classical U-shaped relationship. The result shows how the chosen complexity measure can change the apparent shape of generalization, with the formal characterization established for the random-feature estimators studied rather than for every deep network.
neurips-2025-the-varphi-curve-the-shape-.tldr: For random-feature estimators, norm-based capacity analysis recovers a U-shaped generalization curve without double descent.

paragraphs: Event histories often mix fundamentally different kinds of information. A medical record, for example, can contain categorical procedures alongside continuous laboratory measurements. Forcing everything into tokens can discard useful structure, while imposing one uniform format can mean ignoring some observations. This paper proposes a unified model that accommodates mixed event types.

The framework uses a marked temporal point process implemented with one autoregressive transformer. Separate discrete and continuous prediction heads handle variable-length sequences with flexible event structures. The continuous head uses a normalizing flow to represent continuous attributes, avoiding the numerical integration for inter-event times required by most competing methods.

Experiments report improved prediction quality on both discrete-only and mixed-type sequences, together with interpretable uncertainty quantification. The approach brings different attribute types into a shared sequence model while retaining distinct mechanisms for predicting them. Its contribution is therefore both representational and computational: it accommodates heterogeneous records and changes how continuous quantities are modeled within the event-prediction process.
neurips-2025-transformers-for-mixed-type.tldr: A unified transformer models mixed discrete and continuous event sequences using specialized prediction heads and a normalizing flow.

paragraphs: Adam is widely used, but its advantage over stochastic gradient descent lacks a comprehensive theoretical explanation. This paper studies what happens when the coordinate system of a model's parameter space is rotated. Such tests reveal whether an explanation captures properties tied to the particular basis in which optimization occurs.

In transformer training, random rotations degrade Adam's performance. The authors also identify structured rotations that preserve or improve it. Together, these observations show that rotation matters in a selective way: different changes of basis produce different outcomes. Assumptions that are unchanged by every rotation therefore cannot fully explain the observed advantages.

The paper examines existing rotation-dependent assumptions and finds that they also fail to account for behavior across the tested rotation types. Orthogonality of the update emerges as a promising indicator of Adam's basis sensitivity. The contribution is a sharper empirical and conceptual target for future theory, with update orthogonality proposed as a potentially useful quantity rather than an already complete explanation of Adam's success.
neurips-2025-understanding-adam-requires.tldr: Adam's differing responses to parameter-space rotations expose gaps in current theory and suggest update orthogonality as a promising explanatory quantity.

paragraphs: Reasoning chains have helped language models, but applying them to tasks involving both images and text raises additional questions. Existing approaches often organize reasoning at a coarse level, making intermediate steps difficult to evaluate. This paper investigates a finer chain-of-step formulation so that training can assess the quality of individual reasoning steps.

The framework combines step-level reasoning data, a process reward model, and reinforcement-learning training. The process reward model supplies fine-grained feedback about intermediate reasoning, supporting both learning and inference-time scaling. Bringing these components together provides a transparent framework for studying how step-level supervision affects vision-language reasoning.

The resulting models show consistent improvements on challenging vision-language benchmarks. Empirical analyses and ablation studies examine the contribution of individual components and properties of inference-time scaling. These findings establish a baseline for the proposed approach and offer evidence about how its parts interact. The authors also make the dataset, reward model, and code available, supporting further investigation of structured multimodal reasoning.
neurips-2025-unveiling-chain-of-step-rea.tldr: The paper combines step-level data, process rewards, and reinforcement learning to improve and analyze vision-language reasoning.

paragraphs: End-to-end driving systems combine perception, prediction, and planning, but camera placement can vary between vehicles. Those viewpoint changes create a generalization challenge. VR-Drive addresses it by jointly learning three-dimensional scene reconstruction as an auxiliary task, using that reconstruction to synthesize views in a way connected to planning.

Its feed-forward approach generates training-time augmentations online from sparse views without extra annotations. A viewpoint-mixed memory bank supports temporal interaction across viewpoints. A complementary distillation strategy transfers knowledge from original views to synthesized ones, encouraging consistent behavior when the same scene is observed differently.

Training the system end to end helps reduce the effects of synthesis noise and improves planning under viewpoint shifts. The authors also release a benchmark dataset for evaluating end-to-end driving at novel camera viewpoints. The reported results support VR-Drive as a scalable approach to this robustness problem. Its practical significance lies in making viewpoint variation part of the learning process and providing a dedicated way to measure performance under that variation.
neurips-2025-vr-drive-viewpoint-robust-e.tldr: VR-Drive combines planning-aware view synthesis, cross-view memory, and distillation to improve end-to-end driving under camera viewpoint shifts.
